listeningParts.title: Enrolling on a weather course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A recently retired man phones an adult education centre to book a place on a course about weather.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Hilltop Adult Education Centre, Ruth speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I picked up a leaflet about a weather course you're running this winter, and I'd like to find out a bit more about it, and possibly book a place.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. That'll be Reading the Sky, our introductory course on weather and forecasting. It's designed for complete beginners, so you don't need any background in science. Is it for yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it is. I've just retired, and I spend a lot of my time sailing now, so I'd like to understand the weather properly. At the moment I just look at an app on my phone and hope for the best.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Well, you'd be in good company. Last year about half the group were sailors or hill walkers. The course runs for eight weeks, and there are two options. There's a daytime class on Tuesday mornings, or an evening class on Thursdays, from seven until nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Now that I'm not working, the daytime one would suit me better. I'm not at my best in the evenings. What time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Half past nine, and it finishes at twelve, with a short break for coffee in the middle. The first session is on the fourteenth of January. The evening group starts a week later, on the twenty-first.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The fourteenth. Right. And where exactly is it held? At your main building on the High Street?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No, this course is held at our smaller site, the Ashcombe Building. That's A-S-H-C-O-M-B-E. We use it because it has a flat roof, where the tutor has set up a small weather station. Students take readings from the instruments during every session, so by the end you'll have two months of your own records. It's on Mill Lane, about five minutes' walk from the railway station.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. And what does the course actually cover?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In the first few weeks, you learn to identify the main types of cloud and what they tell you about the weather that's coming. Then you move on to air pressure and wind, and how to read the weather charts you see on television. In the final two weeks, everyone produces their own forecast for the local area, and then compares it with what actually happens. People usually find that part quite humbling.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I can imagine. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full price is ninety-five pounds for the eight weeks. There's a reduced price for people over sixty, which is seventy pounds, and for students, which is fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I turned sixty-two last month, so I think that's me.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Then it's seventy pounds. There's also a course book, which costs twelve pounds. You'll need it from the first week, although some people borrow a copy from the library instead.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll buy one, I think. I like writing notes in the margins.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Fine. I'll add that to the booking. And you'll need to bring a notebook and a pencil, rather than a pen, because pens don't work very well outside in the rain. Oh, and bring a warm coat. You'll be up on the roof for part of every session, whatever the weather is doing.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Of course. That's the whole point, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, could I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Graham Pelling. P-E-L-L-I-N-G.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Pelling. And your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Forty-three Orchard Road, Hilltop.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And may I ask how you heard about the course? We like to know which kinds of advertising work.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: As I said, I picked up a leaflet. It was in the café at the sailing club, down by the harbour.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely, I'll make a note of that. Now, there's a maximum of sixteen students, and at the moment there are only three places left on the Tuesday class, so I'd recommend paying today if you want to be sure of your place.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll do that now. Can I pay by card over the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, that's fine. And one more thing: at the end of the course there's an optional visit to the regional forecasting office near the airport, where you can watch professional forecasters at work. It's on a Saturday, and there's no extra charge, but you have to arrange your own transport.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Excellent. I wouldn't miss that for anything.

listeningParts.title: A tour of a hilltop weather observatory
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a weather observatory that has been recording the weather for over a century.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Carrick Hill Observatory. My name's Siobhan, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we go outside, I'll give you a little background and explain what you'll see on the tour.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The observatory was founded in 1889 by a group of local doctors and teachers who were interested in the weather. You might wonder why they chose such an exposed spot, a good forty minutes' walk from the town. It wasn't for the view, I'm afraid. In those days the town was full of factories, and the smoke from their chimneys affected the readings from the instruments, especially the ones measuring sunshine. Up here, the air was clean, and that's still true today.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Since then, the weather has been recorded here every single day, which makes our records among the longest unbroken series in the country. Scientists studying climate change use them a great deal, because they show how temperatures and rainfall have changed over more than a century in the same place, with the same kind of instruments.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Nowadays, most of the measurements are taken automatically and sent to the national weather service every minute. But we still have two human observers on duty every day. People sometimes ask why we need them, and the answer is that there are things machines still don't do well. A computer can measure rainfall perfectly, but it isn't very good at recognising different types of cloud, or judging how far you can see through mist. So our observers go outside every hour and record what they see.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the different parts of the site. First, there's the Instrument Garden, which is the fenced area of grass you passed on the way in. That's where the thermometers are kept, inside white wooden boxes that protect them from direct sunlight. You can look over the fence, but please don't go inside, because even the heat from a group of people standing close by can change the readings.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to that is the Balloon Shed. Twice a day, at exactly the same times as hundreds of other stations around the world, we release a large balloon filled with gas. It carries a small instrument package that measures temperature, humidity and pressure as it rises, and sends the data back by radio. The balloon expands as the air gets thinner, and eventually it bursts, usually more than twenty kilometres up. The package then falls back to earth on a small parachute. There's a label on each one asking whoever finds it to post it back to us, and you'd be surprised how many people do. The next launch is at a quarter past eleven, so you'll be able to watch it.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: After that, we'll go into the main building. On the ground floor is the Old Library, where you can see the original handwritten record books from the 1880s onwards. They're very fragile, so they're kept in glass cases, but some pages have been scanned, and you can turn them on the touch screens.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Upstairs is the Forecast Studio. This is the part that children usually love most. We've built a copy of a television weather set, with a green screen, so you can try presenting the forecast yourself and take a video home with you. Do try it. It's much harder than it looks.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, there's the Roof Platform, which has wonderful views across three counties on a clear day. Unfortunately, it's closed this morning, because the wind is too strong. I should mention that the strongest gust ever recorded here was a hundred and sixty-one kilometres an hour, during a storm in January 1974, and the anemometer that measured it is on display in the café.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Speaking of the café, it's open until four, and the hot soup is excellent after a morning in this wind. Right, any questions before we start? No? Then follow me, and please do keep your hats on.

listeningParts.title: Testing traditional weather sayings
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two students, Megan and Daniel, discuss their project on weather folklore with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've chosen weather sayings for your project. Tell me how it's going.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Quite well, I think. The idea came from my grandfather, actually. He was a farmer, and he had a saying for everything. Whenever we went for a walk he'd look at the sky and tell us what the weather would do the next day, and he was right surprisingly often.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: So we wanted to find out two things. First, how well people today still know these sayings, and second, whether any of them actually have a scientific basis.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. How did you approach the first question?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: We wrote a short questionnaire listing ten common sayings, and asked people to tick the ones they'd heard of. We collected a hundred and twenty responses, mostly online, although we also stood outside the library for a couple of afternoons to get some older people.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That was sensible. Online surveys tend to attract younger people. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: By far the best known was 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning'. Almost everyone knew it, whatever their age. But with most of the others, there was a clear pattern. People over sixty knew roughly three times as many sayings as people under thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: What surprised us was where people said they'd learned them. We expected the answer to be parents or grandparents, but a lot of the younger people said they'd learned them from books or films.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. And the science?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, the red sky one does seem to have some basis, at least in places like Britain. Weather systems here usually move from west to east. If the sky is red at sunset, it means the sunlight is shining through clear air to the west, where the weather is coming from, so the next day is likely to be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Whereas a red sky in the morning means the clear air is already in the east, moving away, and cloud may be on its way from the west. It's not perfect, but it's not nonsense either.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What about the others?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The one about cows lying down before rain had almost no evidence to support it. We found one study of cattle, but it suggested they lie down mainly when they're tired or the temperature is low, not because rain is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: The most fun part was the pine cones. There's an old belief that pine cones close up before wet weather. We kept three cones on a windowsill for a month and photographed them every morning, and they really did close when the air was damp and open when it was dry.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So they respond to humidity rather than predicting rain, strictly speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Exactly. They tell you what the air is like now, which is often a sign that rain is close, but they can't see into the future.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important distinction, and you should make it clearly in your report. Now, are there any weaknesses in your study that you're aware of?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The main one is the sample. A hundred and twenty isn't very many, and nearly all of them live in the same city. Sayings probably vary from region to region, especially in farming areas.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then say so in your conclusion. It doesn't weaken the project as long as you're honest about it. And for the pine cones, you could compare your photos with the humidity readings from the university weather station. That would make your results much more convincing than just saying the air felt damp.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Good idea. I didn't know the university had a weather station.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It's on the roof of the geography building, and the data's online. Right, I'd like a full draft in three weeks, please, and keep the introduction short. Don't spend two pages on your grandfather.

listeningParts.title: The layers of the atmosphere
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory earth science course on the structure of the Earth's atmosphere.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're going to look at the structure of the atmosphere, the thin layer of gas that surrounds the Earth and makes life possible. And I do mean thin. If the Earth were the size of an apple, the part of the atmosphere where almost all our weather happens would be no thicker than the apple's skin.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Scientists divide the atmosphere into layers, and the main way they do this is by looking at how the temperature changes as you go up. Within some layers the air gets colder with height, and within others it gets warmer, and the boundaries are where that pattern changes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The lowest layer is the troposphere. This is where we live, and it's where nearly all weather happens: clouds, rain, snow and storms. It contains around three quarters of the total mass of the atmosphere, and almost all of its water vapour. In the troposphere, temperature falls steadily as you climb, by about six and a half degrees Celsius for every kilometre. That's why mountain tops are cold, even near the equator. The troposphere isn't the same thickness everywhere. It's only about eight kilometres deep over the poles, but up to around eighteen kilometres over the tropics, because the warm air there rises much higher.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The top of the troposphere is called the tropopause, and it acts a bit like a lid. Clouds can't easily rise through it, which is why the tops of big thunderstorm clouds often spread out into a flat shape, rather like an anvil. Just below the tropopause, you'll also find the jet streams, which are narrow bands of very fast wind, and which airlines use to save fuel when they fly from west to east.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Above the tropopause is the stratosphere, which stretches up to about fifty kilometres. Here, something unexpected happens: the temperature starts to rise with height. The reason is ozone. The stratosphere contains the ozone layer, and ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, which warms the air around it. That absorption is also what protects living things on the surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation. Because warm air sits on top of cooler air, the stratosphere is very stable, with almost no vertical movement and very little cloud, so passenger jets often cruise in its lower part to avoid turbulence.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Above the stratosphere, from about fifty to eighty-five kilometres, is the mesosphere. Here the temperature falls again, and the top of the mesosphere is the coldest place in the whole atmosphere, often below minus ninety degrees Celsius. The mesosphere is also where most meteors burn up. Every day, tons of dust and small rocks from space hit the atmosphere, and the friction heats them until they glow and vaporise. Those are the shooting stars you see on a clear night. Oddly enough, the mesosphere is one of the least studied parts of the atmosphere, because it's too high for aircraft and weather balloons, but too low for satellites to orbit.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Above that is the thermosphere, which extends to several hundred kilometres. In the thermosphere, temperatures can reach well over a thousand degrees Celsius, because the few gas molecules there absorb intense radiation from the Sun. But if you were up there, you wouldn't actually feel hot. The air is so thin that there are hardly any molecules to transfer that heat to your body. The thermosphere is where the International Space Station orbits, at around four hundred kilometres, and it's also where the aurora occurs, the spectacular curtains of green and red light seen near the poles, when particles from the Sun collide with gases in the upper atmosphere.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, the outermost layer, the exosphere, gradually fades away into space, with no clear upper edge. For legal and practical purposes, though, many organisations treat a height of one hundred kilometres, known as the Kármán line, as the boundary where space begins.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, why does all this matter to a meteorologist? Well, although weather happens in the troposphere, the layers above it influence what goes on below, for example through the way the stratosphere affects the jet streams. Next week, we'll look at how air moves within the troposphere, and how those movements create the pressure systems you see on weather maps.

readingPassages.title: The man who named the forecast
paragraphs: Today it is difficult to imagine a world without weather forecasts. They appear on our phones, on television and in newspapers, and millions of decisions, from whether to carry an umbrella to whether a ship should leave port, depend on them. Yet the first forecasts to be published regularly in a British newspaper appeared only in 1861. They were the work of a naval officer named Robert FitzRoy, whose determination to save lives at sea brought him public fame, bitter criticism and, eventually, a lasting place in the history of science.

FitzRoy was born in 1805 into an aristocratic family and joined the Royal Navy as a boy. He is best remembered today as the captain of HMS Beagle during its voyage around the world between 1831 and 1836, on which the young Charles Darwin sailed as a naturalist. The voyage made Darwin famous, but it also confirmed FitzRoy's reputation as a skilled surveyor and a careful observer of the weather. Years of commanding ships in dangerous waters had shown him how many sailors lost their lives in storms that, he believed, could have been anticipated. After a short and difficult period as governor of New Zealand in the 1840s, he returned to Britain, where his interest in the weather would shape the rest of his career.

In 1854, FitzRoy was appointed head of a small new department of the Board of Trade, the government body responsible for commerce and shipping. This department, which later became known as the Met Office, had a limited purpose at first. It was not expected to predict the weather at all, but to collect information about winds and currents at sea, so that voyages could be made faster and safer. FitzRoy supplied the captains of merchant ships with reliable instruments and asked them to keep detailed logs of the conditions they met. These records were then gathered in London and turned into charts.

A disaster in October 1859 changed the direction of his work. A violent storm swept across Britain, and the Royal Charter, a ship returning from Australia, was wrecked off the coast of Anglesey in north Wales. Hundreds of passengers and crew drowned, and many other vessels were lost around the coast. Studying the reports afterwards, FitzRoy became convinced that the storm's approach could have been detected in advance. What made this possible was a relatively recent invention: the electric telegraph. For the first time, observations of pressure, wind and temperature from places hundreds of kilometres apart could be collected within hours and compared, rather than arriving days later by post.

In February 1861, FitzRoy began sending storm warnings by telegraph to ports around the British coast. When a warning was received, a large canvas cone was raised on a tall pole where sailors could see it, its position indicating the expected direction of the wind. Later that year, he went further. On 1 August 1861, The Times newspaper printed his first general weather forecasts for different regions of the country. FitzRoy is usually credited with introducing the word 'forecast' in this sense; he wanted a term that sounded like a reasoned scientific judgement rather than a prophecy.

The forecasts quickly became popular with the public, and fishermen in particular came to depend on the storm warnings. FitzRoy also arranged for barometers to be placed in fishing ports, so that crews could check the pressure themselves before putting to sea, and he explained how to interpret the readings in simple language. In 1863 he published The Weather Book, in which he set out his methods and his conviction that the weather, although complicated, followed patterns that could be understood.

However, the forecasts also attracted fierce criticism. When they were wrong, as they often were, newspapers mocked them and questions were asked in Parliament. Many scientists argued that FitzRoy's methods relied too heavily on personal judgement and lacked a proper theoretical basis. Some ship owners complained that the warnings kept their vessels in harbour unnecessarily, costing them money. FitzRoy, who was overworked, in poor health and deeply hurt by the attacks, died in 1865. Shortly afterwards, a committee appointed to review the department concluded that the forecasts could not be scientifically justified, and they were stopped in 1866. The storm warnings, however, were restored after protests from coastal communities, and newspaper forecasts eventually returned more than a decade later.

FitzRoy's reputation has risen steadily since then. Modern forecasting relies on far more data and far more powerful methods than he could have imagined, but the basic idea he championed, that observations gathered quickly from a wide area can be used to warn people of the weather to come, remains at its heart. In 2002, when the sea area called Finisterre in the Shipping Forecast broadcast on BBC radio needed a new name to avoid confusion with a Spanish area of the same name, it was renamed FitzRoy in his honour.

readingPassages.title: Calculating tomorrow
paragraphs: Every day, the world's major weather services feed millions of observations from satellites, aircraft, ships, balloons and ground stations into some of the most powerful computers on Earth. These machines solve the equations that describe how air moves, warms, cools and condenses, and the result is a picture of the atmosphere hours, days and even weeks ahead. The idea behind this process, known as numerical weather prediction, is more than a century old, but it took decades of failure, ingenuity and technological progress before it became the foundation of modern forecasting.

The starting point is usually traced to 1904, when the Norwegian scientist Vilhelm Bjerknes argued that forecasting should be treated as a problem in physics. If the present state of the atmosphere were known accurately enough, he reasoned, the laws governing the motion of fluids and the behaviour of heat could be used to calculate its future state. The principle was elegant, but there was an obvious difficulty. The equations involved were far too complex to be solved exactly, and approximate solutions required an enormous amount of arithmetic, at a time when every calculation had to be done by hand.

The first person to attempt it seriously was the British mathematician Lewis Fry Richardson. During the First World War, while serving as a driver with an ambulance unit in France, he spent his spare time working out, by hand, how the pressure and winds over a small part of central Europe would change over six hours, using observations recorded on a single day in 1910. The task took him many weeks. When he finally finished, his result was spectacularly wrong: he predicted a rise in surface pressure of 145 hectopascals, a change far larger than any ever observed, when in reality the pressure had barely altered. Richardson nevertheless published his method, together with his failed result, in his 1922 book Weather Prediction by Numerical Process.

Rather than abandoning the idea, Richardson imagined how it might one day work in practice. He described a vast hall, shaped like a theatre, in which 64,000 people, each responsible for one part of the globe, would carry out calculations simultaneously, while a conductor in the centre used beams of light to keep them working at the same pace. This 'forecast factory' was never built, but it anticipated with remarkable accuracy the way modern supercomputers divide the atmosphere into a grid of points and process them in parallel. Much later, researchers who repeated his calculations showed that his method had been largely sound; the error came mainly from problems with the starting data, which contained small unrealistic variations that the equations magnified.

The arithmetic finally became manageable with the arrival of electronic computers. In 1950, a team in the United States that included the meteorologist Jule Charney and the mathematician John von Neumann used ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, to produce a series of forecasts for North America. The model was greatly simplified, and producing a 24-hour forecast took roughly 24 hours of computing time, so it was of no practical use. But the forecasts were reasonably realistic, and they proved that the approach could work. By the middle of the 1950s, weather services in Sweden and the United States had begun issuing computer-based forecasts routinely.

Just as the method was proving its worth, a discovery revealed its limits. In 1961, the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz was running a simple weather model on a computer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Wanting to examine one result again, he restarted the run part-way through, typing in a number from a printout, 0.506, instead of the full value of 0.506127 stored in the machine. The tiny difference grew until the new simulation bore no resemblance to the original. Lorenz realised that the atmosphere is chaotic: very small uncertainties in its starting state grow rapidly, so that detailed forecasts eventually become impossible, however good the model. A later talk in which he asked whether the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas gave the phenomenon its popular name, the butterfly effect.

Forecasters responded not by giving up but by changing how they work. Since observations can never be perfect, modern weather centres run their models not once but dozens of times, each starting from slightly different conditions that reflect the uncertainty in the data. This technique, called ensemble forecasting, became part of daily operations in the early 1990s. When the different runs produce similar results, forecasters can be confident; when they spread widely, the forecast is uncertain, and that uncertainty can itself be communicated to the public.

The results of these advances have been striking. Studies suggest that forecasts have gained roughly a day of useful accuracy with each decade, so that a five-day forecast today is about as reliable as a three-day forecast was some twenty years earlier. Most scientists believe, following Lorenz, that the limit for detailed day-to-day forecasts lies at around two weeks. More recently, technology companies and weather centres have developed systems based on machine learning, which are trained on decades of past weather data and can produce forecasts in minutes rather than hours. Whether these will replace traditional models or simply work alongside them is one of the most important questions facing the field.

readingPassages.title: A thirty per cent chance of confusion
paragraphs: Weather forecasts have never been more accurate. Thanks to satellites, supercomputers and decades of research, a forecast for three days ahead is now roughly as reliable as a forecast for the next day was a generation ago. Yet complaints that 'the forecast is always wrong' remain as common as ever. In my view, the main problem with weather forecasting today is not the science, which is remarkably good, but the way its results are communicated to the people who rely on them.

Consider the familiar 'thirty per cent chance of rain'. In a study published in 2005, the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer and his colleagues asked people in five cities, Amsterdam, Athens, Berlin, Milan and New York, what such a forecast actually means. The answers varied enormously. Some people thought it meant that it would rain for thirty per cent of the time, while others believed it would rain over thirty per cent of the region. The meaning intended by forecasters, that it will rain on about thirty per cent of days with a forecast like this one, was far from universally understood. Residents of New York, where forecasts of this kind had been broadcast for decades, were the most likely to choose it.

Confusion is not only the fault of the public. In his 2012 book The Signal and the Noise, the statistician Nate Silver described what forecasters call the 'wet bias'. Examining American forecasts, he found that the national weather service's probabilities of rain were well calibrated, but that many local television forecasters deliberately exaggerated the chance of rain, because viewers who are caught in an unexpected shower are angrier than viewers who stay indoors because of rain that never arrives. I find this understandable, but in my opinion it is self-defeating: an audience that discovers it has been misled, however kindly, has less reason to believe the next warning, which may be one that really matters.

Graphics can mislead as well as words. Forecasts of hurricanes approaching the United States are often shown with a 'cone of uncertainty', a shape that widens over time to show where the centre of the storm is likely to travel, based on the size of past forecasting errors. The cone is a sensible way of displaying uncertainty, but research has repeatedly found that many people read it as a map of the area that will be affected, and conclude that if they live outside it they are safe. In fact, the cone says nothing about the size of a storm, and dangerous winds and flooding often extend far beyond its edges.

Some weather services have tried to address such problems by changing what a warning is about. The UK's Met Office, for example, now issues impact-based warnings, coloured yellow, amber or red. The colour depends not only on how likely severe weather is, but on what it is expected to do: whether it is likely to close roads, cut off power or endanger lives. A heavy snowfall that would be a minor inconvenience in a mountain village might therefore lead to a higher warning in a city where it rarely snows. I believe this is exactly the right approach, because people make decisions about what the weather will do to them, not about rainfall totals.

Another innovation has been less obviously useful. Since 2015, the Met Office and Met Éireann, Ireland's weather service, have given names to major storms, a practice long established for hurricanes. The aim is to raise awareness and make it easier for the media and the public to follow a storm's progress. The names certainly attract attention, and they make headlines easier to write. Whether they actually change how people prepare is, as far as I am aware, much less clear, and I suspect that a memorable name can sometimes make a storm seem like entertainment rather than a threat.

A more radical argument is that the public simply cannot cope with uncertainty, and should be given clear, simple messages: rain or no rain, safe or unsafe. This view is understandable but, I think, mistaken. Research by the psychologist Susan Joslyn and her colleagues at the University of Washington has found that people who are given probability information alongside a forecast tend to make better decisions, and to trust the forecast more, than people who receive a simple prediction. Uncertainty does not confuse people when it is explained clearly; what confuses them is uncertainty presented in ways they cannot interpret.

In my view, the next great advance in forecasting will come not from faster computers but from taking communication as seriously as calculation. Forecasters already know a great deal about how much they do not know. The challenge is to share that knowledge honestly, and in a form that helps people decide whether to cancel a journey, move their livestock or leave their homes. That will require meteorologists to work closely with psychologists, designers and the communities they serve.
